title: Hubble Frontier Fields view of MACSJ0416.1–2403
caption: The galaxy cluster MACS J0416.1–2403, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
credit: NASA, ESA and the HST Frontier Fields team (STScI)

recognition.text: Official ESA/Hubble press-release image. No published audience rating.

story: This Hubble image shows the galaxy cluster MACS J0416.1–2403, one of six clusters studied by the Hubble Frontier Fields program. As a set, those clusters have given astronomers their deepest ever views of gravitational lensing.

The cluster contains so much mass that it bends the light of objects lying behind it. In effect, it acts as a huge magnifying lens. Light from more distant galaxies passes close to the cluster, is deflected by its gravity, and arrives at Hubble brighter and larger than it would otherwise appear.

Astronomers have used this natural lens to look very far back in time. Using this cluster and two others, they found galaxies dating from a time when the Universe was only 600 to 900 million years old, counting from the Big Bang. Light from such galaxies has been traveling for most of the history of the Universe, so these objects show the Universe when it was young.

understand.summary: This image combines visible and near-infrared observations from Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys and Wide Field Camera 3. The color assigned to each filter is not published.
understand.eye: Much of this light is near-infrared, invisible to the eye, and the distant lensed galaxies are far too faint to see without very long telescope exposures.

explore: The cluster lies in the direction of the constellation Eridanus. Lensed background galaxies often appear stretched or smeared, because the cluster's gravity distorts their light as well as magnifying it.
alt: A dense field of galaxies in a massive cluster, with many smaller, fainter galaxies scattered across a dark background.
